summary:
Delta State stands under Nigeria's national framework, where same-sex conduct has been criminal since 1916. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act, passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law in January 2014, criminalises all forms of same-sex union with a maximum federal penalty of 14 years' imprisonment, and its reach extends to cohabitation between same-sex partners, public shows of a same-sex amorous relationship, the operation of gay organisations, and participants and guests at same-sex weddings. Section 217 of the Criminal Code makes male gross indecency a felony liable to three years' imprisonment. The death penalty for male sodomy is confined to the twelve northern Shari'a states under state Zina provisions. No state-specific protective statute exists in Delta.

Delta has a documented record of mass arrests under this framework. In June 2018 police in Asaba arrested more than 100 party-goers at a hotel on charges that they were gays and lesbians, and by July 2018 they were facing homosexuality-related charges in court. In August 2023 police raided what Wikipedia's overview describes as a gay wedding in Warri, arresting dozens in the case known as the 'Warri 67', of whom 67 were charged to court.

Accounts of the night of 27 August 2023 differ on what occurred. The US State Department's 2023 human rights report, cited in the UK Home Office's June 2025 country policy note, records that Delta police raided a 'white party' organised by the LGBTQI+ community and detained more than 200 individuals, with police alleging the event was a same-sex wedding while some civil society representatives disputed that account. Daily Post reports that officers from Ekpan Division in Uvwie Local Government Area arrested 67 suspects at 9 pm at Teebolus Hotel, Refinery Road, Ekpan, for allegedly conducting and attending a same-sex wedding ceremony between Daniel Pius, 22, and Maxwel Ohwonohwo, 20.

Delta State Police Command spokesman DSP Bright Edafe said the raid followed a confession by a male cross-dresser that he belonged to a gay club and was travelling to a gay marriage ceremony, that the suspects fled on the officers' arrival but 67 were chased and arrested, and that drugs and 'gay marriage ceremonial dresses' were recovered. Edafe said the suspects and exhibits were in custody and efforts continued to arrest fleeing members for possible prosecution. One suspect alleged he had been sexually assaulted by a man at the hotel while intoxicated.

A human rights lawyer based in Warri told the UK Home Office that victims of 'kito' — predatory same-sex assault — under-report for fear of prosecution, which leaves visitors and residents exposed both to the assault and to the machinery used against them. State-level documentation from Delta is thin, and that absence of records does not demonstrate safety.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office travel advisory, reported by Sahara Reporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct, of the death penalty under Sharia law in some northern states, and of the statute's reach to participants and guests at same-sex weddings.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement in Delta is repeatedly packaged with other allegations: the 2023 Warri raid was announced alongside seized drugs, and a cross-dresser's confession about a gay club served as the stated predicate for the operation. Visitors whose conduct is unrelated to drug offences can nonetheless be drawn into that framing.

Press coverage and police statements in Delta use gender presentation as evidence. The command spokesman's account rested on a male cross-dresser's confession, and press descriptions of wedding parties identify a 'bride' and 'groom' by dress, which places visibly gender-nonconforming people at the centre of such raids regardless of what occurs at the event.

The reporting risk runs both ways for someone assaulted: the Warri lawyer's account of kito under-reporting indicates that victims expect prosecution under the same statute as their attackers. The absence of state-level statistics mirrors the pattern in other Nigerian jurisdictions where official record-keeping about anti-LGBT enforcement is uneven.
localsOnly:
Residents of Delta live under the national statute rather than a local ordinance, so Delta State Police Command divisions enforce the 2014 Act and Section 217 of the Criminal Code, and there is no state protective instrument to invoke before a Delta court.

Charges in Delta have followed large social events rather than private conduct alone: the Asaba hotel arrests of June 2018 and the Ekpan arrests of August 2023 both proceeded against attendees, and the Warri 67 were committed to court after a single night's operation.

Residents who report assault face exposure under the same law their attackers used. The Warri-based lawyer's statement to the UK Home Office is the on-the-ground position: kito victims do not come forward because reporting risks a homosexuality charge.

The police command's public statements about these operations come from its spokesman, DSP Bright Edafe, who described suspects and seized exhibits in custody and continued efforts to arrest those who fled.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources conflict on the character and scale of the raid of 27 August 2023 in Warri/Uvwie: one records a 'white party' with more than 200 detained and a civil-society dispute over the police account, while others record a same-sex wedding at Teebolus Hotel with 67 arrested and 67 charged. Whether these describe one event with divergent counts or separate operations is unresolved in the material available here.

Outcomes are not sourced. The disposition of the Asaba 2018 charges after July 2018, and the final result of the 'Warri 67' prosecutions, are not recorded here.

Nigeria-wide proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public were reported in 2022; whether any such proposal has been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Detention conditions, access to legal representation for those charged in Delta, and any protection or remedy available to a visitor detained under the statute are not covered by this inventory.
